seo_desc: Pain under your big toe joint? Our podiatrists in Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens diagnose and treat sesamoiditis and sesamoid fractures. Call (561) 915-1934.
lede: A dull ache under the ball of your foot, right below the big toe, is often sesamoiditis, and offloading those two small bones usually brings relief.
what_it_is: Under your big toe joint sit two tiny bones, each about the size of a corn kernel, tucked inside the tendons that bend the big toe. These sesamoid bones work like pulleys, helping the tendons glide and absorbing force every time you push off. Sesamoiditis is irritation and inflammation of these bones and the tendons around them, usually from repeated pressure on the ball of the foot.

AAOS OrthoInfo notes that it is most common in dancers, runners, and baseball catchers. Cleveland Clinic adds people who often wear high heels and people with high arches or bunions, and the American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons points to high-impact sports such as basketball and tennis. Because the pain sits under the big toe, it is easy to confuse with a stress fracture of the sesamoid or with turf toe.
symptoms: Pain under the big toe on the ball of the foot
A dull ache that builds gradually or gets sharper over time
Pain that flares with certain shoes or activities
Trouble bending or straightening the big toe
Difficulty putting weight on the ball of the foot
Mild swelling, tenderness, or sometimes bruising under the joint
causes: Repeated pressure on the ball of the foot from running, dancing, or court sports
Frequent high-heel wear, which shifts weight onto the forefoot
High arches that load the front of the foot
Bunions or other changes at the big toe joint
A sudden bend-back injury of the big toe
Thin or worn-out shoes with little cushioning

how_therapy_helps.intro: Treatment centers on taking pressure off the sesamoids so the inflamed tissue can settle. AAOS OrthoInfo describes rest from the aggravating activity, anti-inflammatory medication, ice, soft-soled or stiff shoes, felt pads, and taping the big toe slightly downward, with a short-leg fracture brace for four to six weeks if symptoms persist. OrthoInfo notes that most sesamoid problems resolve without surgery. The American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons also lists immobilization, physical therapy, cortisone injections, and custom orthotics.
methods: Felt or foam pads shaped to sit around the sesamoids shift pressure away from the sore spot, and J-shaped pads are used when a fracture is involved.
Taping the big toe so it stays slightly bent, or wearing stiff-soled shoes, limits motion at the joint and reduces strain on the sesamoids.
When symptoms persist, OrthoInfo describes a short-leg fracture brace for four to six weeks to fully rest the area.
Oral anti-inflammatory medication and ice help with pain and swelling, and a steroid injection may be considered for more severe inflammation.
Custom orthotic devices, which ACFAS describes for long-term treatment, help balance the pressure on the ball of the foot once you are back on your feet.
For chronic sesamoiditis that does not respond to care, or a sesamoid fracture that will not heal, part or all of the affected sesamoid can be removed or repaired.

first_visit: Your podiatrist presses directly on each sesamoid to see whether the tenderness is in the bones or elsewhere in the ball of the foot, then moves the big toe up and down to check range of motion and pain. Your gait, arch type, and the wear pattern on your shoes are reviewed. X-rays, sometimes of both feet for comparison, help tell sesamoiditis apart from a fracture, and an MRI or bone scan may be ordered if X-rays look normal.
recovery: Recovery varies widely. Cleveland Clinic says mild sesamoiditis can improve within days once you stop stressing the area, while severe cases can take months to fully heal. AAOS OrthoInfo explains that healing is often slow because every step loads the forefoot, and that recovery can mean several weeks or months in a cast or brace. Returning to running or dance too soon is a common reason symptoms come back, so build activity up gradually.
self_care: Take a break from running, jumping, and dancing on the ball of the foot
Wear low-heeled shoes with a cushioned or stiff sole, and skip high heels and thin flats
Ice the area for short sessions with a cloth barrier
Avoid going barefoot on hard tile or pool decks while it is sore
see_a_doctor: Pain under the big toe that does not improve with rest
Pain that started suddenly after a fall, jump, or the big toe bending back hard
Significant swelling or bruising under the big toe joint
Trouble walking or bearing weight on the ball of the foot
Pain that interferes with regular daily activities

faqs.q: How do I know if I have sesamoiditis or a sesamoid fracture?
faqs.a: Both cause pain under the big toe joint, and they can feel similar. Sesamoiditis usually builds slowly as a dull ache, while a fracture often follows a specific injury or causes sharper pain and swelling. AAOS OrthoInfo explains that X-rays help separate the two, and that a bone scan or MRI may be needed because some stress fractures do not show on X-ray.

faqs.q: How long does sesamoiditis take to heal?
faqs.a: It depends on how inflamed the area is. Cleveland Clinic says mild cases can start improving within days of taking stress off the ball of the foot, while severe cases may take months. AAOS OrthoInfo notes that some people need a brace for four to six weeks. Continuing high-impact activity on a sore sesamoid tends to slow healing.

Most people can walk, but the goal is to walk without loading the ball of the foot. Stiff-soled or cushioned low-heeled shoes, a felt pad around the sesamoids, and taping can make walking more comfortable. If walking is painful even with these changes, a podiatrist may recommend a boot or brace for a few weeks to let the area rest.

faqs.q: How do you tape for sesamoiditis?
faqs.a: AAOS OrthoInfo describes taping the big toe so it stays bent slightly downward, and the American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons notes that taping or strapping the toe relieves tension on the area. AAOS also describes pairing it with a felt or dense foam cushioning pad. Because tape that is too tight or placed wrong can cause new problems, it is best to have a podiatrist show you the technique first.

faqs.q: Are high heels bad for sesamoiditis?
faqs.a: Yes, high heels push body weight forward onto the ball of the foot, right where the sesamoids sit. Cleveland Clinic lists frequent high-heel wear as a risk factor and recommends avoiding overly high heels and narrow toe boxes. While the area heals, low-heeled shoes with good cushioning or a stiff sole are a better choice.
